plan: Complete enhanced-ACT social-science passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000041, 'Thirty-Eight Witnesses'), about 600 words, on the bystander effect: the 1964 Genovese report, Darley and Latané's experiments, later corrections to the story, Philpot et al. (2019) camera study, and a reconciliation of individual and group likelihood. Topic checked against all ACT Reading and SAT R&W passages (no bystander/Genovese passage). 10 questions. Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: R041-06 medium→easy, R041-08 medium→easy, R041-09 hard→medium, R041-10 hard→medium.

passages.title: Thirty-Eight Witnesses
passages.text:
In March 1964, a young woman named Kitty Genovese was attacked and killed near her apartment building in Queens, New York. Two weeks later, the New York Times reported that thirty-eight of her neighbors had seen or heard the attack and that none of them had called the police until it was over. The story became a national symbol of the indifference of city life, and it inspired a generation of research on why people fail to help strangers in trouble.

Among the first researchers were the psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané. In a series of experiments in the late 1960s, they staged emergencies—a participant might overhear what sounded like another student having a seizure, for example, or sit in a room that slowly filled with smoke—and measured how quickly people responded. Their central finding was striking: people who believed they were alone usually helped, and helped quickly, while people who believed others were present were less likely to help at all. Darley and Latané proposed two explanations. When many people witness an emergency, each may feel less personally responsible, assuming that someone else will act. And each may look to the others for cues; if no one else seems alarmed, the situation may not seem like an emergency. The pattern came to be called the bystander effect.

The bystander effect has been reproduced in many laboratory studies, and it became one of the best-known findings in psychology. But the story that launched it turned out to be less accurate than it first appeared. Later investigations, including reporting by the Times itself, concluded that the number of witnesses had been exaggerated, that few if any of them saw the whole attack, and that at least one neighbor had called the police and another had gone outside to help.

More recently, researchers have asked whether the laboratory finding holds in real emergencies at all. In a study published in 2019, a team led by the psychologist Richard Philpot examined security-camera footage of more than two hundred public conflicts—arguments and fights—recorded in cities in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and South Africa. In about nine of every ten conflicts, at least one bystander stepped in, whether by gesturing to calm someone down, pulling an aggressor away, or comforting a victim. And the more bystanders were present, the more likely it was that someone intervened.

These findings do not necessarily contradict the laboratory research. The bystander effect concerns the likelihood that any particular individual will help, and a person in a crowd may indeed be less likely to act than a person alone. But a victim needs only one helper. A crowd can contain many people who hold back and still, as a group, be more likely than a single witness to produce someone who steps forward. If so, the lesson of the bystander research may be less about human indifference than about how responsibility gets divided—and how, often enough, it does not disappear.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: A famous news story from 1964 proved that people living in large cities are less willing to help strangers than people living in small towns.
choices.B: Laboratory studies of the bystander effect have been shown to be false by recent research using security cameras.
choices.C: Research prompted by a famous but flawed news story found that individuals in groups help less, yet groups as a whole often do produce a helper.
choices.D: Psychologists now agree that people are more likely to help in an emergency when they are alone than when others are present.

candidates.evidence: These findings do not necessarily contradict the laboratory research.
candidates.explanation: The passage traces the bystander research from the Genovese story through laboratory findings, the story's flaws, and real-world camera data, and ends by reconciling individual reluctance with group helping.

A.rationale: The passage says the story was exaggerated, and it never compares cities with small towns.

B.rationale: The passage says the camera findings "do not necessarily contradict" the laboratory research.

D.rationale: The passage ends by suggesting that crowds as a whole are often more likely to produce a helper.

hints: How does the last paragraph connect the earlier findings?
candidates.remember: A main idea must fit the passage's conclusion as well as its opening.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the first paragraph is to:

choices.A: describe a widely reported event that led researchers to study why people fail to help.
choices.B: argue that the New York Times should not have reported the attack on Kitty Genovese.
choices.C: explain the two causes of the bystander effect proposed by Darley and Latané.
choices.D: present evidence from security cameras that bystanders usually intervene.

candidates.evidence: it inspired a generation of research on why people fail to help strangers in trouble
candidates.explanation: The first paragraph recounts the Genovese case as reported in 1964 and says it inspired research on bystanders, setting up the rest of the passage.

B.rationale: The paragraph reports what the Times said; it does not argue about whether it should have reported it.

C.rationale: The explanations appear in the second paragraph.

D.rationale: The camera study appears in the fourth paragraph.

hints: What does the paragraph say the story inspired?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the rest of the passage needs from this opening.

candidates.remember: Opening paragraphs often supply the background that motivates the passage.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, one explanation Darley and Latané offered for the bystander effect is that when many people witness an emergency, each person:

choices.A: may be too frightened by the size of the crowd to move toward the victim.
choices.B: may not have a telephone nearby with which to call the police quickly.
choices.C: may believe that the victim is only pretending to be hurt or in danger.
choices.D: may count on another witness to take action instead of doing so personally.

candidates.evidence: each may feel less personally responsible, assuming that someone else will act
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says each witness "may feel less personally responsible, assuming that someone else will act."

A.rationale: The passage does not mention fear of the crowd.

B.rationale: Phones are never mentioned as an explanation.

C.rationale: The passage does not offer this explanation.

candidates.remember: Detail questions are answered by a specific sentence.

candidates.stem: Based on the second explanation Darley and Latané proposed, a participant in the smoke-filled room who sees two other people calmly continuing their work would most likely:

choices.A: leave the room immediately to report the smoke.
choices.B: conclude that the smoke is probably not a sign of danger.
choices.C: ask the two others whether they feel responsible for the smoke.
choices.D: assume that the two others have already reported the smoke.

candidates.evidence: if no one else seems alarmed, the situation may not seem like an emergency
candidates.explanation: The second explanation is that people read others' reactions; calm companions signal that nothing is wrong, so the participant would likely decide the smoke is not dangerous.

A.rationale: The explanation predicts the opposite: calm companions make the situation seem less urgent.

C.rationale: The explanation concerns reading others' reactions, not questioning them.

D.rationale: That reflects the first explanation (shifting responsibility), not the second (reading cues).

hints: What does the second explanation say people do?

strategy.explanation: Identify which explanation the question names.

candidates.remember: When a question names one of two explanations, eliminate the choice that fits the other.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "staged" most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: The researchers set up fake emergencies to observe responses, so "staged" means arranged.

B.rationale: Although "stage" can mean a step, the researchers set up emergencies, not steps.

C.rationale: The emergencies were set up in experiments, not performed on a stage.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the emergencies were postponed.

hints: What did the researchers do with the emergencies?

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the sentence, not the most familiar one.

candidates.stem: The third paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: prove that laboratory studies of the bystander effect could not be reproduced.
choices.B: introduce the security-camera study that tested the bystander effect in real life.
choices.C: explain why the bystander effect became well known among psychologists.
choices.D: show that the news story that prompted the research was less accurate than first reported.

candidates.evidence: the story that launched it turned out to be less accurate than it first appeared
candidates.explanation: After noting the effect's fame, the paragraph reports that later investigations found the Genovese story exaggerated.

A.rationale: The paragraph says the effect "has been reproduced in many laboratory studies."

B.rationale: The camera study is introduced in the fourth paragraph.

C.rationale: Its fame is mentioned in one clause; the paragraph focuses on flaws in the original story.

hints: What does "But" introduce in this paragraph?
candidates.remember: A paragraph's purpose is usually stated right after a turn word like "But."

candidates.stem: According to the passage, in the conflicts that Philpot's team examined, at least one bystander intervened in about:
candidates.evidence: In about nine of every ten conflicts, at least one bystander stepped in
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 states that in about nine of every ten conflicts, at least one bystander stepped in.

B.rationale: The passage says about nine of every ten, not one.

C.rationale: The passage gives about nine of every ten, far more than half.

D.rationale: "About nine of every ten" means some conflicts had no intervention.

candidates.remember: Quantity questions are answered by an exact figure in the passage.

candidates.stem: Compared with Darley and Latané's experiments, Philpot's study differed mainly in that it:

choices.A: measured how quickly individual participants responded to what sounded like a seizure.
choices.B: examined real conflicts recorded in public rather than emergencies set up by researchers.
choices.C: found that no bystanders ever intervened in conflicts where large groups were present.
choices.D: relied on the reporting of the New York Times to identify and interview the witnesses.

candidates.evidence: whether the laboratory finding holds in real emergencies at all
candidates.explanation: Darley and Latané staged emergencies in experiments; Philpot's team analyzed footage of real public conflicts to see whether the laboratory pattern holds outside the lab.

A.rationale: That describes one of Darley and Latané's experiments.

C.rationale: Philpot's team found that intervention became more likely as the number of bystanders grew.

D.rationale: The study used camera footage, not newspaper reports.

hints: Where did each study's emergencies come from?
candidates.remember: Comparison questions turn on a real difference, not a detail of one study.

candidates.subskill: Applying an argument to new evidence
candidates.stem: Which of the following hypothetical findings would be most consistent with the reasoning in the last paragraph?

choices.A: Lone witnesses helped less often than individuals in groups did, and victims with only one witness were also helped less often.
choices.B: Each bystander in groups of ten helped less often than lone witnesses, and victims with ten bystanders were also helped less often.
choices.C: Bystanders in groups helped exactly as often as lone witnesses did, and the size of the group made no difference to how often victims were helped.
choices.D: Each bystander in groups of ten helped less often than lone witnesses did, yet victims with ten bystanders were helped more often than victims with one.

candidates.evidence: A crowd can contain many people who hold back and still, as a group, be more likely than a single witness to produce someone who steps forward.
candidates.explanation: The paragraph combines two claims: each individual in a crowd is less likely to help, but the crowd as a whole is more likely to contain a helper. Only D shows both.

A.rationale: This contradicts the laboratory finding the paragraph accepts, that individuals in crowds are less likely to act.

B.rationale: The paragraph argues that groups as a whole can be more likely to produce a helper, not less.

C.rationale: The paragraph accepts that individuals in crowds are less likely to act, so no difference would not fit its reasoning.

hints: What two claims does the last paragraph combine?

strategy.explanation: State the paragraph's reasoning in your own words first.

candidates.remember: To apply an argument, find the choice that matches every part of its reasoning.

candidates.stem: The author's attitude toward the bystander effect is best described as:

choices.A: accepting that it is a real finding about individuals while questioning what it has been taken to show about people in general.
choices.B: dismissive, because the news story that first inspired the research turned out to be exaggerated and partly false.
choices.C: uncritical, because the effect has been reproduced in many laboratory studies over several decades of research.
choices.D: puzzled, because the laboratory findings and the security-camera findings seem impossible to reconcile with each other.

candidates.evidence: the lesson of the bystander research may be less about human indifference than about how responsibility gets divided
candidates.explanation: The author accepts the laboratory finding about individuals ("a person in a crowd may indeed be less likely to act") but suggests its lesson is not human indifference.

B.rationale: The author says the effect has been reproduced many times and does not dismiss it.

C.rationale: The author raises questions about its real-world meaning, so the view is not uncritical.

D.rationale: The author explicitly reconciles the two sets of findings in the last paragraph, so the author is not puzzled by them.

hints: Does the author reject the finding or reinterpret it?

strategy.explanation: Look at the author's own words in the last paragraph.

candidates.remember: Attitude questions usually have a measured answer; watch for extreme words.

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves matched every key; both flagged that R041-07 (Philpot's method) and R041-08 (lab vs real conflicts) tested the same point. Replaced 07 with a detail item on the nine-in-ten intervention rate; reworded 03's key so it does not copy the passage; replaced one extreme distractor in 10 ('hostile') with a moderate wrong attitude ('puzzled') so the key is not the only non-extreme choice; changed 'outside her apartment building' to 'near' (the fatal attack was inside the building). Whole batch re-solved blind.
